#5312. RBC Signals brings in $10M investment to expand strategic frontiers for satellite services

by Alan Boyle on Nov 19, 2026 at 6:33 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 6:33 pm

Redmond, Wash.-based RBC Signals has announced a $10 million strategic growth investment aimed at accelerating the company’s expansion into government satellite data services and the commercialization of emerging space technologies.

RBC Signals supports satellite operators by arranging access to a global network of ground stations, including its own assets and antenna facilities operated by partners.

In August, for example, Blue Origin and RBC Signals announced a partnership to build out the ground infrastructure for Blue Origin’s Quartz communications network. RBC Signals is also a provider for the U.S. Space Force’s Joint Antenna Marketplace.

The newly announced investment was led by Washington Harbour Partners, a private investment firm based in Washington, D.C. The firm ranked sixth among all defense technology investors in the Silicon Valley Defense Group’s 2026 NatSec100 Report.

“Our vision has always been to build a global, secure network of networks that makes space connectivity more accessible, flexible and reliable,” Ron Faith, RBC Signals’ president and CEO, said today in a news release.

“By bringing together infrastructure, partners and emerging technologies, we’re creating a dual-use platform that can evolve alongside the needs of the national defense and the commercial space industry,” Faith said. “This investment from Washington Harbour Partners will help us accelerate that vision by expanding our government services business and bringing emerging capabilities such as higher frequency bands, optical connectivity, intersatellite links and space domain awareness to market.”

Mina Faltas, founder and CEO of Washington Harbour Partners, highlighted RBC Signals’ role in addressing the growing demand for space connectivity. “We see tremendous potential in the company’s ability to deliver mission-critical capabilities, and we’re excited to support the team as they enter this next phase of growth,” Faltas said.

#5311. This Is the Reason Your AI Tools Actually Remember Anything

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

These are the two AI tools I used to ensure mine ran smoothly, efficiently and retained the right knowledge.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

During the World Cup this year, I built Rune Score, a sports analytics chatbot. From the outside, it looks like a simple chatbot. Under the hood, it’s a distributed system that has to handle the freshness of sports data, user rephrasing, extraction failures, LLM call costs, streaming, memory, fallbacks and security. What I learned building it applies to almost any AI product that has to stay fast, cheap and accurate at the same time.

Two quick definitions before we go further, since neither tool is exactly a household name. Redis is “an open-source, in-memory data structure store used as a database, cache, message broker and streaming engine,” most commonly used in AI products as a fast cache that stores one exact answer under one exact label. RAG, short for retrieval-augmented generation, is defined by AWS as “a technique used to augment a large language model (LLM) with external data, such as a company’s internal documents.” Instead of matching an exact label, it searches for a broader knowledge base using meaning rather than exact wording. Redis is precise and cheap but rigid. RAG is more flexible and durable, but costs more to run.

My first move wasn’t a vector database, it was a Redis cache built around a simple labeling rule: Identical requests get an identical key, something like the football matchup Argentina vs. Spain. The savings were immediate. As I documented in my LinkedIn article on Rune Score, “without the cache, a fresh extraction followed by an analysis can consume up to 23,000 input tokens: scraped content, context, history. With a cache that hits the same key, that number drops to about 5,000 tokens,” a 4.5-fold reduction in the single most expensive part of the pipeline.

AI cost usually comes from what you repeat unnecessarily. If 10 people ask your product the same question within a reasonable time window, rerunning the full, expensive pipeline 10 times is money burned for no reason.

People don’t talk in fixed labels. They might write “FC Barcelona vs Real Madrid,” or “Barça – Madrid,” and a strict cache treats each variant as a completely different request. That means duplicate work, a missed answer that was already sitting there or an unnecessary rerun of the whole expensive pipeline just because the wording didn’t match.

This is where RAG earns its place, through a technique called embeddings. According to Google Cloud’s documentation, “the closer objects are in the embedding space, the more semantically similar they are, and greater distances indicate greater semantic dissimilarity.” In plain terms, a knowledge base built this way can retrieve a past answer even when the question is worded completely differently, because it searches by meaning rather than exact wording.

Here’s a lesson worth internalizing regardless of what you’re building: The biggest quality bottleneck in a RAG system usually isn’t the retrieval technology itself; it’s what feeds it. This is the classic computing idea that TechTarget defines as garbage in, garbage out, or GIGO, “the idea that in any system, the quality of output is determined by the quality of the input.” In my pipeline, every time I cut corners on how much content got extracted from a source, the resulting analysis got visibly worse downstream.

The same logic applies to how the system ranks relevance. Trusting a single relevance score is fragile. Redis’s own engineering blog puts it plainly: “the consistent takeaway across these studies is that combining retrievers tends to surface more relevant results in the top positions than either method on its own.” Combining exact keyword matches, meaning-based search and how recent the information is, then merging those into one ranking, beats relying on any single signal alone.

In my experiment with Rune Score, RAG hit brings a request down from 20,000 to 8,000 tokens — a 60% reduction. Compared to the 80% reduction from an exact Redis hit, that’s less economical and slightly slower, but that gap isn’t a strike against RAG. What it buys instead is tolerance for how people actually phrase things, memory that outlives a cache’s expiration window and an architecture that’s reusable well beyond the one product you built it for.

Redis and RAG aren’t competing choices; they’re sequential ones. The best refactor isn’t the one that’s theoretically right; it’s the one that lets you roll back in seconds if the real metrics don’t hold up. Build the cheap, fast cache first, let it teach you what your users actually ask for and only then invest in a full retrieval system for the cases a cache structurally can’t handle.

During the World Cup this year, I built Rune Score, a sports analytics chatbot. From the outside, it looks like a simple chatbot. Under the hood, it’s a distributed system that has to handle the freshness of sports data, user rephrasing, extraction failures, LLM call costs, streaming, memory, fallbacks and security. What I learned building it applies to almost any AI product that has to stay fast, cheap and accurate at the same time.

Two quick definitions before we go further, since neither tool is exactly a household name. Redis is “an open-source, in-memory data structure store used as a database, cache, message broker and streaming engine,” most commonly used in AI products as a fast cache that stores one exact answer under one exact label. RAG, short for retrieval-augmented generation, is defined by AWS as “a technique used to augment a large language model (LLM) with external data, such as a company’s internal documents.” Instead of matching an exact label, it searches for a broader knowledge base using meaning rather than exact wording. Redis is precise and cheap but rigid. RAG is more flexible and durable, but costs more to run.

My first move wasn’t a vector database, it was a Redis cache built around a simple labeling rule: Identical requests get an identical key, something like the football matchup Argentina vs. Spain. The savings were immediate. With a cache that hits the same key, that number drops to about 5,000 tokens,” a 4.5-fold reduction in the single most expensive part of the pipeline.

#5310. John Deere acquires Orchard Robotics, an AI farming startup with Seattle ties

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 20, 2026 at 7:52 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:14 am

Orchard Robotics, an agtech company using artificial intelligence to help growers monitor crops and make farming decisions, has been acquired by John Deere. The deal was announced Thursday and the terms were not disclosed.

The startup has developed a system of cameras mounted on tractors and other equipment that gather images as the machines traverse a farm. Orchard’s AI analyzes the images to generate data on vines, trees and crops, which is then used to track growth, yield and health.

“This acquisition connects crop-level intelligence with John Deere technology and equipment that can precisely execute the work in the field,” Tim Marquis, John Deere’s director of farm systems innovation, said in a statement.

That includes helping farmers target treatments and make better-timed decisions about thinning, spraying and harvesting.

Orchard was founded by CEO Charlie Wu, a Thiel Fellow who dropped out of Cornell University to launch his business in 2022.

“Over these next few years, our goal is to bring the power of Orchard’s industry-leading technology and AI Farming capabilities to every farmer out there,” Wu said in a LinkedIn post. “This is only the beginning of a long and awesome journey ahead.”

The startup is based in San Francisco and has an office in Seattle. Wu splits his time between the two cities and was a finalist for Young Entrepreneur of the Year at the 2026 GeekWire Awards.

Orchard has raised more than $25 million from investors, including a $22 million Series A round announced in September 2025. The startup has 45 employees, according to PitchBook.

The Pacific Northwest is home to numerous agtech startups. That includes other companies that collect and analyze data, such as Loftus Labs and innov8.ag, as well as IUNU and Koidra, which are focused on greenhouse crops. Businesses tackling field operations include weed destroyers Carbon Robotics and Aigen; rock-removing TerraClear; and irrigation startups FarmHQ and Verdi.

#5309. AI Is Helping Your Team Do More. That Doesn’t Mean They Can Handle More.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Your team may be busy thanks to AI, but robotic productivity is a poor substitute for outstanding human performance.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Companies that begin using AI tools are definitely seeing a productivity boost. However, as team production increases, team performance dips.

What’s the cause? AI helps to make task completion faster. At face value, that sounds beneficial since human workers don’t need to spend as much time getting their work done. But there’s been a huge problem: Organizations are responding by increasing workloads and expectations.

The result is that teams are getting more work accomplished, but individual employees aren’t getting any kind of a break. On the contrary, they’re expected to multiply their workloads — and that’s a surefire road to capacity strain and burnout.

Maybe you’ve noticed this phenomenon as you’ve begun to introduce AI adoption among team members. Are they struggling to prioritize and adapt? Do they have trouble making sound decisions amid an environment that makes it tough to distinguish healthy efficiency from unsustainable acceleration? If you’ve said “yes,” you’re not alone. That said, you’ll probably want to take action today to make sure your team members aren’t becoming cognitively overwhelmed by the technology that’s supposed to alleviate their stressors by doing repetitive tasks on their behalf.

The workplace has become increasingly complex, and employees don’t necessarily have intuitive skills that will help them know how to appropriately adapt. For instance, consider a team member who shifts 20% of his regular work to AI-based processes. Does the team member innately know how to make the most of the 80% of his work that remains? Or understand what he can do to fill in the 20% with high-value assignments that only a human can do?

Organizations can address this challenge by helping employees better regulate their attention and mental state under pressure. This does not mean teaching people how to think critically from scratch. It means helping them create enough cognitive space to apply the judgment, adaptability, and emotional intelligence they already possess. For example, human performance company Q Studio, takes this approach through organization-wide Mind Skills Training designed to help professionals sustain clearer thinking and stronger performance in this new paradox.

On a broader level, corporate agile training company Agile Seekers works with companies interested in teaching their team members how to show curiosity and skepticism regarding AI. Instead of simply accepting what AI recommends, employees learn to look for errors and ask questions. Consequently, they are able to use their brains to thoughtfully engage with AI work rather than accept it without question.

As teams start to embrace AI, individual employees may stop communicating as much. Essentially, they allow AI software and systems to complete work, and then simply pass the products through the process. This begins to erode the human connection, which can lead to disengagement and burnout.

It’s very difficult for teams to perform at optimal levels if individuals aren’t committed to working together. Therefore, it’s up to you as a leader to set the expectation that AI implementation isn’t an excuse for building siloes or allowing subpar work. After all, Thomson Reuters research shows that when employees are given the okay to just turn in AI work, they lose a sense of connection with that work — and, eventually, with each other.

You hired your team because of the talent that each employee brings to your organization. The best way to bring out their collective performance is by keeping them in close contact. And sometimes that means turning away from AI products. For example, there are now chatbots trained to help managers practice having difficult conversations. However, encouraging team members to role play with each other can be a stronger way to build bonds, support and comfort.

Are leaders around the world laying off team members in the name of AI? Yes, for certain. (Some giants aren’t, though.) However, that’s a tricky move. Even if you feel like AI has improved your team’s productivity, reconsider downsizing.

When you let people go because AI “took their jobs”, you send a mixed signal to everyone who remains in your organization or department. From their point of view, productivity is more important to you than performance. Accordingly, they may stop trying to hand in stellar work and just try to be as busy as possible.

If you really want your employees to focus on being high performers, downsize very carefully. Otherwise, you could end up with a lot of team members who get plenty of error-prone work done under the guise of being productive.

Certainly, productivity will always matter, and AI can allow your employees to do more work in less time. But make sure you’re not concentrating so hard on getting more done thanks to AI that you forget to celebrate the special human characteristics and acumen that only your team members can provide.

Companies that begin using AI tools are definitely seeing a productivity boost. However, as team production increases, team performance dips.

What’s the cause? AI helps to make task completion faster. At face value, that sounds beneficial since human workers don’t need to spend as much time getting their work done. But there’s been a huge problem: Organizations are responding by increasing workloads and expectations.

The result is that teams are getting more work accomplished, but individual employees aren’t getting any kind of a break. On the contrary, they’re expected to multiply their workloads — and that’s a surefire road to capacity strain and burnout.

#5308. StepSecurity, led by two Microsoft vets, raises $20M to defend developers’ tools from hackers

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 20, 2026 at 8:28 amNovember 20, 2026 at 8:34 am

StepSecurity’s co-founders spent more than two decades combined at Microsoft. This week, as their startup announced a new round of funding, its researchers were also investigating a hacked Microsoft software package.

Their old employer is not the only one with this problem.

StepSecurity, a Seattle-area cybersecurity startup, raised a $20 million Series A round led by Elephant, with participation from existing investors Runtime Ventures, Inner Loop Capital and SaaS Ventures. The company has now raised $23 million, including a $3 million seed round in 2024. Axios Pro first reported the latest round.

The startup protects the systems used to build software: developers’ laptops, code repositories, package downloads and CI/CD pipelines, the automated systems that assemble and ship code.

The problem is that attackers increasingly slip malicious code into open-source software that developers download. That code can do damage as soon as it runs on a developer’s laptop or build system, stealing the passwords and keys that unlock other systems.

“A supply chain attack used to take a skilled team,” CEO Varun Sharma wrote in a blog post announcing the funding. “Now one person can vibe code it.”

Sharma spent about 15 years at Microsoft, where he led a team in Azure Security focused on making security easier for developers. CTO Ashish Kurmi spent nearly eight years at Microsoft before leading cloud security at Uber and infrastructure security at Plaid.

The two met at Microsoft and started StepSecurity in 2021, after working through the fallout from the SolarWinds and Codecov supply chain attacks at their respective employers.

A busy week: The Microsoft package, agent-framework, is the Python version of Microsoft’s open-source toolkit for building AI agents.

It gets roughly 190,000 downloads a month. Two malicious versions published on Nov. 17 to PyPI, the main public repository for Python software, included code designed to steal cloud and CI/CD credentials as soon as Python started up, SecurityWeek reported. PyPI quarantined both versions, and a Microsoft maintainer said an investigation was underway.

That’s one entry in a long list. StepSecurity’s announcement also cites the $6.3 billion Binance breach in October, which the FBI attributed to North Korea’s TraderTraitor group. Binance has said the attack started with a compromised employee laptop.

It also points to a tampered copy of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension that sat in Cursor’s extension marketplace for about 11 hours last month. Cursor said up to 5,000 users may have received the malicious version.

StepSecurity says it documented 56 confirmed compromises of trusted software components between August 2025 and August 2026, and roughly one every three days from March 2026 through the August report.

How it works: StepSecurity got its start with its own tool, Harden-Runner, which is free for open-source projects. It watches automated builds on GitHub and flags anything unexpected in the processes they run, the network connections they make or the files they change.

More than 20,000 open-source projects use it, the company says, up from about 3,000 at the time of the seed round. Unusual behavior spotted in those public builds has helped StepSecurity catch attacks early, the company says, including the March 2025 compromise of tj-actions, a widely used add-on for GitHub’s build automation.

StepSecurity’s paid products also protect developers’ laptops and check code repositories. Its Secure Registry service screens software packages before a company’s builds download them from public sources such as npm, the main public repository for JavaScript packages. It blocks versions known to be compromised and holds brand-new releases for a waiting period, giving researchers time to catch malicious ones before anyone installs them.

Along with the funding, StepSecurity is making Secure Registry free for public GitHub projects that use Harden-Runner and run their builds on GitHub’s servers. The free version defaults to a two-day waiting period and supports JavaScript packages, with Python, Java, Ruby and Rust planned.

StepSecurity has plenty of competition. Socket, a San Francisco startup that screens open-source packages for malicious code, raised $60 million at a $1 billion valuation in May. Sonatype, JFrog and Endor Labs also sell tools that can block risky packages before they’re installed.

Growth spurt: StepSecurity says its annual recurring revenue grew fivefold in 2024, fivefold again in 2025 and more than fivefold so far this year. It didn’t disclose dollar figures.

Named customers include Circle, Dexcom, Kong, Mercari, Chainguard and XBOW.

The company has 27 employees, up from four, including the founders, at the time of the seed round. Sharma is based in Sammamish and Kurmi in Kirkland, and the rest of the remote-first team is spread across the U.S., Canada and India.

What’s next: StepSecurity plans to extend its protections to agent sandboxes, the isolated environments where AI agents run code. Its argument is that anyone who asks an AI agent for a spreadsheet may be downloading and running open-source packages.

The company says it also plans to double its team over the next 12 months, mostly in security research, engineering and sales and marketing.

#5307. How the surge in AI-discovered bugs is straining Microsoft security and threatening tech stability

by Angela Gunn on Nov 20, 2026 at 9:25 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:25 am

It has come to the attention of the general public this month that adversaries successfully adopt technology a lot faster than defenders do. This has nothing to do with the willingness of defenders to try. It has everything to do with the ancient truth that to succeed, defenders have to get it right every time but adversaries only have to get it right occasionally.

Now multiply “every time” and “occasionally” by AI. Do you like that math? Does anyone?

The disastrous update that broke Teams, Outlook, SharePoint and other packages was not a direct attack by AI-wielding bad guys. Nor was the FAA outage. Nor were most of the outage events of the past few weeks, though who can say what’s up with those European Union refrigerators.

No. The true AI-driven mayhem has been predicated for several months now not on powerful new AI-honed attacks, but on an absolute deluge of bugs of relatively low severity that Microsoft and other defenders with a formal patch process aren’t built to process.

The question is whether traditional patch programs can adapt their processes to handle the deluge. Microsoft’s is MAPP (Microsoft Active Protections Program), to which the company has been committed for nearly two decades. If the industry-spanning events of the past few weeks are any indication, these programs can’t.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said Wednesday at the New York Times DealBook Summit that last week’s Microsoft 365 outage came from a latent bug and wasn’t directly tied to AI, but he warned that AI-driven patching could bring more instability.

He elaborated in a separate appearance on CNBC the same day, saying the flood of patches being applied to older infrastructure is making systems less stable.

AI has “allowed us to find these bugs and fix these bugs, but that means you’ve got to then patch them, and that creates instability,” Nadella said, when asked by Jim Cramer about a string of recent outages at United, Schwab, Chase and other organizations.

Some context: MAPP turned 18 this year. The program, run by the MSRC (Microsoft Security Response Center), handles outreach to partner companies that gain early access to information on the bugs in advance of each month’s Patch Tuesday release. In-house, it coordinates the patch release process, just as the larger MSRC organization helps coordinate the handling of bug reports from external finders.

MSRC also runs point on prioritizing patches of the worst bugs through its SSIRP (Software and Services Incident Response Plan) program, itself dating to 2004. In its time, it was an industry leader in how companies can efficiently get their arms around bad bugs.

MAPP in its own way is similarly remarkable. It has undergone a few traumas over the years, usually when a partner breaks confidence and leaks the advance details it receives. In 2025, after attacks on SharePoint raised suspicions of a leak from the program, Microsoft stopped giving Chinese companies early access. But MAPP continues to tick along in a way that would make any program manager proud. Other companies have their own version of MAPP / MSRC, as do community efforts such as those supporting Linux.

Full disclosure: I’m a former MSRC employee who learned about MAPP at the knee of the program’s principals. I subsequently tracked patch releases at a company partnered with MAPP at its highest (Validate) level, which means I was privy to the 14-day multi-stage run-up to each month’s release. I admire and respect the program… and I’m afraid that in the AI-finder era, it’s in big, big trouble.

Since January 2021, Microsoft has issued patches for an estimated 10,319 CVEs. (I use estimated numbers throughout this analysis because there are various ways of counting such things, including whether or not the patch accrues to an application such as Edge, which actually relies on the Chromium project for its fixes. Other analysts arrive at larger or smaller counts.)

Over half of those — 5,383 CVEs — are 2026 releases, 5,128 of which were addressed since April. In comparison, 2025’s full-year CVE total was 1,180.

What happened in April? As nearly as analysis can determine, the floodgates opened and finders (security researchers) started barraging the company with reports.

The first quarter of 2026 saw 255 CVEs addressed over three months. April had 163, May 132; in June the number jumped to 209. In July it was off to the races with 575 CVEs. In October, the monthly count topped 1,400.

Most of these bugs aren’t coming from the usual security stalwarts. They’re coming from new finders, they’re coming in with multiple simultaneous finders not believed to be working together, and they’re coming in relatively weak.

Though the overall volume has skyrocketed, the number per month of bugs under active exploit in the wild — the notorious “zero-days” — hasn’t increased proportionally.

Moreover, average bug severity has in fact decreased. Until 2026, the average CVSS severity score for all bugs tended to hover around 7.8 (out of 10) each month. In 2026, that’s dropped to approximately 7.4 as of September — not garbage finds, but the sort of thing that doesn’t scramble the jets.

No surge in zero-days and a drop in severity — that’s good news. The problem is the volume.

Once bugs are received by Microsoft, each goes through a MAPP-helmed, multi-team process of investigation and patch development.

The true AI-driven mayhem has been predicated not on powerful new AI-honed attacks, but on a deluge of bugs of relatively low severity that Microsoft and others aren’t built to process.

Since many products have several versions still in support, that often means that multiple teams within each product group are asked to ingest a bug report, replicate the problem, devise and test a fix, ensure the fix doesn’t trigger other problems or inadvertently point to a similar bug elsewhere in the product and ready it for mass consumption. Even AI slop has to be taken seriously, just in case.

Meanwhile, MAPP is the traffic cop for the entire release, working with each team to ascertain patches are ready, understand the nature of the bugs and what can be safely communicated to partners and the public, and ready the processes that make the second Tuesday of each month a festival of downloads and reboots. From where we stand right now, it’s all fairly… hand-crafted.

In theory the process is automatable to some extent, though the success of that effort so far in light of recent events is debatable. But high volume also leads to other problems, such as exposing information on incomplete patching.

For instance, Microsoft has recently patched Office bugs that apply to both Windows and Mac, but patches have initially only been available for Windows versions.

Microsoft’s release-day information about such bugs — patching Windows versions while asking Apple users to monitor Microsoft communications for news of their own patch — alerts the world, including eager adversaries, that the flaw exists. Apple customers just have to hope no adversaries exploit it while their patch is pending.

More broadly, many of the steps in the current patching process involve judgment calls, not processes that scale well or that can reliably be handled by existing AI-driven systems. In Microsoft’s case, MAPP is a remarkably small team of humans and, being security folk at Microsoft, they’re not always the loudest or most popular voice in Redmond.

Add the mercurial nature of finders, who may or may not provide full details on their bugs (ask any MSRC person how often they receive a crash dump and a demand for payment) and may or may not disclose their finds publicly if they don’t feel they’re getting sufficient response.

Do not add the kind of defender staffing needed to handle a massive increase in volume — either in MAPP or in the individual product groups building the actual patches — because in the AI era, it’s likely the companies won’t add it either.

The cracks are showing. Microsoft has been compelled to issue OOB (out-of-band) releases and servicing updates monthly since July, often within just a few days of the original release.

OOBs are important enough to merit release outside the usual patch cadence, often because there’s a security issue involved, but they’re tough on administrators already wading through a slew of regularly scheduled patching. With volumes high, patch testers may rush or elide certain steps, such as checking that a fix doesn’t break something deeper in the system.

Nadella told the DealBook audience this week that a patch for a critical bank system might once have been tested for a week. Now, he said, the patch “needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild. So that’s going to create instability.”

Think of MAPP as Mariners catcher Dan Wilson in 2001: a pro handling a staff of skilled human pitchers, one pitch at a time. Now it’s 2026, and the pitchers have been swapped for a bank of mediocre pitching machines all slinging fastballs at … 2026-era Dan Wilson.

Here, again, AI can’t fix a system that requires defenders to catch every pitch. Secondary lines of defense that have worked in the past — for instance, the requirement by various regulatory programs that enterprises ascertain that patches are safe for their own systems — rely heavily on companies sending out the soundest possible patches.

Managed service providers might at least make sure that patches are flagged to customers as available, relevant and urgent. But they’re in no position to do much more than trust that what’s shipped is safe to deploy and react when things go wrong.

Even that gets harder when a bug kneecaps the security tools they depend on. Last week’s Microsoft 365 outage affected parts of Microsoft Defender that interact with Exchange Online.

It’s not just Microsoft, of course. The Linux community is seriously suffering, and both Apple and (especially) Google have struggled with patch-release quality in 2026 as evidenced by their own emergency updates and post-release device instability reports. Industry-wide, ecosystems built around reliable, transparent patch cadences and patch-development processes have never seemed more in danger of being overwhelmed.

What needs to happen? Sure, build those AI systems; the marketing people will be pleased. It’ll speed up some parts of the process. But a system capable of replicating, every time, the human judgment calls that go into the patch-release process isn’t going to magically create itself; people have to create it.

Is there some chance that the deluge will ebb — that researchers and their tools will at some point finally find all the bugs in all the world’s products?

It’s a pretty thought, and some relief may eventually come. When more and more unrelated finders turn up the same bug, it gives one hope that the set is finite. But no one knows when relief will come, and most folk in tech suspect that really, no, there is no bottom to the bug barrel. Nor, for the foreseeable future, any rest for the weary.

#5306. Startup Spotlight: An engineer’s search for better, safer baby products led him to launch Birch

Startup Spotlight profiles tech startups in the Pacific Northwest.

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 20, 2026 at 9:41 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:41 am

A new baby can be the ultimate anxiety trigger: When will she sleep through the night? What if nursing is a challenge. What is that rash?! Given the countless unknowns, the last thing a parent needs are worries about the quality of the baby’s crib or the chemicals in a pacifier.

But when Karthik Gangiredla was preparing for the birth of his first daughter, he and his wife spent hours trying to figure out which baby products were trustworthy.

“We struggled a lot,” Gangiredla said. “We did a lot of research on what was safe, what’s not.”

An engineer with roughly 20 years of experience in supply chains and logistics, including roles at Amazon, Flexport and TikTok, Gangiredla found himself on the consumer side of the retail equation, scrutinizing strollers and bottles.

To spare other parents the same headache, he turned that research into Birch, an online marketplace that offers baby product buying guides and assigns each item a TrustScore. Its scoring system draws on certifications, lab reports and recall databases to help parents assess goods ranging from baby wipes to teething toys.

The site provides information on more than 10,000 items across 110 brands, including manufacturing locations, suppliers, certificate numbers and test reports.

Birch has contracts with brands it has checked out, and serves as their merchant of record, meaning if a customer has issues with a product or wants to return it, Birch handles those steps. It operates fulfillment centers in Los Angeles and New Jersey.

Gangiredla said the startup flips the e-commerce approach of retail giants, focusing on the shoppers’ needs, not those of the merchant. It does not accept ads or sponsored rankings.

If you took away the ad revenue for Amazon or TikTok, “the business wouldn’t exist,” Gangiredla said. “So it’s very difficult for them to approach the problem in a different way.”

The platform also offers a gift registry and tools for tracking fetal development during pregnancy, an infant’s nursing and sleep schedules, and other developmental steps. The tools are free for users.

We caught up with Gangiredla, Birch’s CEO and founder, for this edition of GeekWire’s Startup Spotlight.

In 50 words or less, give us your startup’s elevator pitch

Birch is the trust-first platform for baby and kids products and parenting resources. We research and score products across 50+ safety and quality signals before listing — and stock only what clears the bar — so parents skip the endless research and buy with confidence, from pregnancy through the toddler years.

What problem are you obsessed with solving?

The impossible research burden on new parents. Every purchase feels like a safety decision, the information is scattered and often unverified, and the stakes feel enormous. We’re obsessed with moving the work of figuring out what’s trustworthy off the parent and onto a system that does it rigorously — and then showing our work.

What surprised you after talking to customers?

How universal the trust problem is. We assumed it would track with income or with first-time parents, but our customers span all 50 states and every kind of household — big metros to small towns. And what they consistently want isn’t more options or a lower price; it’s someone to tell them, credibly, what’s actually worth buying.

How has AI changed the way you build your company?

It’s core, not a feature. Our TrustScore engine evaluates thousands of products across dozens of safety and quality signals in ways a human team our size never could, and the same intelligence powers discovery and personalization. It also lets a very lean team operate like a much larger one — and we now license that engine to other baby and kids brands as a product called Juno.

What’s one thing people misunderstand about your startup?

That “curated” means limited or expensive. Curation isn’t about carrying less for its own sake, or about selling premium — it’s about removing the untrustworthy. In our own data, price and trustworthiness barely correlate; some of the highest-scoring products are among the most affordable. Fewer and better, not fewer and pricier.

What’s the toughest decision you’ve made in the past year?

Turning away brands and revenue. When you’re early, every dollar is tempting — but our entire promise is that everything on Birch has earned its place. Saying no to products and partners that didn’t clear the bar, even when the revenue was real, was hard. It’s also the decision that defines what we are.

What’s the one piece of advice you give to other entrepreneurs?

Earn trust before you try to scale it. It’s slower and less glamorous than chasing growth, but trust compounds and shortcuts don’t. And talk to your customers far earlier, and far more often, than feels comfortable.

…a parent’s first instinct, the moment they find out they’re expecting, is to come to Birch — and “did you check the TrustScore?” is just how families talk about buying for their kids.

#5304. Microsoft ‘To Do’ users make a big to-do over popular task app’s pending retirement

by Todd Bishop on Nov 20, 2026 at 2:06 pmNovember 20, 2026 at 2:07 pm

Microsoft acquired the popular Wunderlist app in 2015, shut it down in 2020 and told its loyal users that Microsoft To Do would be their new home. Now they’re being asked to pack up again.

Microsoft plans to retire the To Do apps on June 30, 2027, moving personal task management for work and school accounts into Planner, its team project-management app. Microsoft disclosed the change Wednesday in a long Planner blog post amid the company’s Ignite announcements, and Windows Latest flagged the change later that day.

The reaction was swift and mostly unhappy. Tom Warren of The Verge summed it up on X: “Microsoft is killing its great tasks app in favor of its worse tasks app.”

That’s not entirely fair to Planner, which is built for a different job. But it captures the gripe: To Do was simple, free and worked across Windows, Mac, iOS, Android and the web, and nothing Microsoft is offering replaces all of that.

For work and school accounts, Microsoft says Planner “will be the destination for managing personal work tasks,” but “existing To Do tasks and lists will not migrate to Planner.” It says it will offer a way to export To Do data before the app shuts down.

Tony Redmond of Office365itpros, who tracks Microsoft 365 closely, cataloged the gaps: no file attachments on private Planner tasks, no equivalent for To Do’s list groups, no transfer of shared-list membership, assignments or permissions, and no native Planner apps for Windows or Mac.

He also noted the irony that Outlook’s old Exchange-based tasks will outlive To Do.

Why Microsoft is doing it: The company said putting individual and shared work on the same foundation lets it deliver more consistent features, and lets people connect their own tasks to Copilot and other AI agents. A new Planner agent, available with a Copilot add-on license, can take on tasks and generate status reports.

The Register’s Richard Speed put it less charitably, saying Microsoft had slipped the news into “this week’s Ignite AI puffery.”

Users weigh in: Brad Silverberg, the former Microsoft executive who led Windows 95 development and later became a Seattle venture investor, posted on X that he has used To Do daily, and Wunderlist before it.

“Very disappointed now,” he wrote, adding that he’s looking at TickTick and Todoist.

Similar posts piled up on LinkedIn from Microsoft 365 consultants and everyday users, some of them describing Planner as clunky by comparison.

Patrick Husting, a Seattle-area entrepreneur and software developer whose Ghostwriter add-in brought AI to Microsoft Office before Microsoft announced Microsoft 365 Copilot, offered on LinkedIn to maintain To Do for Microsoft for free.

Rivals smell an opportunity: Competitors wasted no time. TickTick posted a migration guide for To Do refugees. Todoist CEO Amir Salihefendic wrote on LinkedIn that the shutdown was “pretty unexpected” and pointed out that his app has outlasted competitors for 20 years.

The most pointed pitch came from Superlist, which called itself “the natural successor” and said it already has a tool for importing To Do lists. Wunderlist founder Christian Reber started the company in 2020.

Reber and his co-founders sold Wunderlist’s parent company, 6Wunderkinder, to Microsoft in 2015 for a reported $100 million to $200 million. In 2019, as Microsoft prepared to shut the app down, he publicly asked Satya Nadella to sell it back. Microsoft kept it, then retired it in favor of To Do.

Now some of those former Wunderlist users may end up back with the people who built it.

US stocks suffered a selloff last night, with the S&P 500 dropping 2.02% to 7,175.83. The Nasdaq Composite lost 2.25%, while the Dow Jones fell 2.19%. More than 90% of S&P 500 companies finished lower.

A slowdown in AI infrastructure spending is affecting companies across the entire supply chain, not just American technology giants.

US spot Bitcoin ETFs are still recording heavy outflows. Another $306.5 million in net outflows yesterday, with seven finalized trading sessions producing $1.4 billion in withdrawals.

Bitcoin ETF outflows now coincide with a reassessment of expensive growth assets, weakening institutional demand just as the crypto market faces additional selling pressure. The AI boom has not disappeared, and Nvidia’s latest results demonstrate that demand remains enormous. But investors are no longer rewarding growth at any price.

#5301. Microsoft’s final Outlook outage report details testing gaps and safeguards that backfired

by Todd Bishop on Nov 21, 2026 at 9:31 amNovember 21, 2026 at 9:50 am

The bug behind last week’s global Microsoft 365 outage struck only newer, more powerful servers in a key part of Microsoft’s network. That’s because it created a kind of traffic jam inside each server, and the more work a machine tried to do at once, the worse the jam got. The newer servers are built to do more at once, so they’re the ones that seized up.

One reason Microsoft didn’t catch it in advance: it was testing on older servers.

“Our testing did not adequately represent the combination of hardware and traffic mix encountered during this incident,” the company acknowledged in its final report, released Friday evening, a week after resolving the outage that crippled Outlook and cut off email for people around the world.

Testing that more closely replicates the company’s production environment is one of 13 next steps in the report — measures the company says it will take to keep it from happening again. The list is also aimed at reassuring the businesses that rely on Microsoft for email and collaboration, after CEO Satya Nadella acknowledged at the company’s Ignite conference this week that it has work to do on resilience.

Many of the other steps identified in the report go after a bigger problem: during the incident, the safeguards meant to contain the failure spread it around the world instead.

What set it off: As detailed in Microsoft’s preliminary report last weekend, the bug at the center of the outage had been sitting dormant since July, when Microsoft started rolling out the software update that introduced it. For more than three months, it caused no problems.

The bug affected the servers that make up what Microsoft calls its network gateway, a front door that connects people to Outlook email and other Microsoft 365 services. The flaw came from a Windows update used only on those servers. Standard versions of Windows weren’t affected.

So what was the bug? Microsoft’s final report gives a partial answer, saying it came from a change to how the gateway servers handle incoming connections.

Under heavy load, it turned out, the Windows process that sets up those connections bogged down, with tasks stuck waiting on each other until the servers ran out of computing power and memory and stopped responding.

The final report doesn’t say what the July update was meant to fix. But it does lay out three conditions that finally set the bug off. Without the bug, even all three together would have been routine, the report says.

First, nearly 14% of the gateway’s server capacity was already offline that day for routine software updates. That’s normally not a problem, because Microsoft keeps enough spare capacity to absorb it. But it meant fewer servers were available to carry the load.

That’s a different explanation from the preliminary report, which blamed the missing capacity on an unrelated problem.

Second, all of Microsoft Teams’ traffic landed on those same servers. Teams normally runs through a separate gateway of its own. About 15 hours before the outage, a routing glitch on that Teams gateway in Microsoft’s US East region set off an automatic switch that moved all Teams traffic worldwide onto the servers that handle email.

Third, the U.S. workday got going. Widespread failures began around 8 a.m. Pacific, as traffic in North America climbed toward its daily peak.

How it spread: As servers stopped responding, Microsoft’s systems automatically moved their traffic to healthy servers nearby, which had the same bug and buckled under the extra load. At the low point, more than 80% of the gateway’s servers in North America were unresponsive.

The system then shifted traffic to other regions, spreading the problem further.

“Within about two hours of the broad failures that began in North America, servers in every region were affected globally,” the report says.

The preliminary report had blamed that spread partly on “a separate issue.” The final report doesn’t repeat or explain that phrase. Instead, its findings say the way Microsoft distributes traffic “can cascade failures to other regions.”

Once the servers went down, getting them back up was its own problem. As servers came back online, they were swamped by pent-up demand and froze again, a pattern engineers call a “thundering herd.” Microsoft says it will ease traffic back onto recovering servers gradually. That fix doesn’t have a date yet.

The fixes: To keep a failure from spreading again, Microsoft says it will change how its systems shift traffic between regions, so a problem in one part of the world stays there.

It also plans to split up the servers that handle email, so a surge from another service like Teams can’t take them down. And Teams will switch over only in the region that has the problem, not worldwide.

Some of the fixes are due by the end of the year, others by the end of March. Several don’t have a date yet.

Microsoft says its first notice to customers went out about 20 minutes after the outage took hold, and it plans to shorten that by the end of the year. No business email was lost, according to the report, though some delayed messages to consumer mailboxes that had been inactive for more than 30 days bounced back to senders.

The report also confirms what Microsoft said the day after the outage began: it wasn’t hackers, and it wasn’t AI. “This incident was confirmed not to be caused by a cyberattack, and we found no evidence of malicious activity,” it says. “This change was not caused by AI tooling.”

The new testing is supposed to be in place by the end of March, according to the final report. This time, the company says, the machines in the lab will actually match the ones running the service in production.

Shiba Inu’s lead ambassador Shytoshi Kusama has stayed silent on social media, with his last post dated May 13, 2026, leaving many questions in the Shiba Inu community.

Kusama remains a prominent figure in the Shiba Inu ecosystem and before then he had frequently communicated with the community about developments, project direction and broader ambitions. His limited public presence, which goes back to mid-2025, has therefore become a talking point for holders who want updates from the project's leadership.

With no confirmed return date or fresh public statement from Kusama, speculation in the community continues. At the start of the year, Kusama revealed he was working on an independent AI project.

His silence on social media hasn't been a complete blackout, as Kusama updates his X location and bio in the meantime. As reported, Kusama changed his X bio to “polish” and his location to “close.”

A low profile on X, however, does not establish that Kusama has left the Shiba Inu project or stopped contributing behind the scenes. No such departure has been confirmed in the information available at press time.

The question remains as to when Shytoshi Kusama will address the community again, with the timing yet unknown.

But the Shiba Inu community might have something to look forward to on November 19, 2026, after a teaser was dropped by a longtime Shiba Inu community member, Mazrael, in an X post.

Mazrael wrote a brief post that said, “Here goes something,” with the “eyes” emoji and a time: November 19 at 11 a.m. UTC.

Though the post did not disclose what is in the works, the timing has sparked the curiosity of Shiba Inu community members, with speculation mounting about a possible announcement or update. At press time, no further details have been provided, and what the teaser leads to remains unknown.

In a separate post, Mazrael shared an update on the MetaMask X ticker widget, which showed copycat tokens for BONE and TREAT, saying that MetaMask was fixing the root cause, not patching tokens one at a time.

SoftBank Group is assembling a rescue financing plan for WeWork that may value the office-sharing company below $8 billion, according to Bloomberg. The new figure is a fraction of the $47 billion valuation the startup commanded as recently as January, and yet it *still* seems a little high when compared with its bigger, profitable, publicly traded rival IWG, whose valuation is roughy half that amount.

Fun fact: Amazon went public in 1997 with $16 million in revenue and a market cap of $438 million. #ThoseWereTheDays. WeWork co-founder Adam Neumann didn’t plan for his family’s control of WeWork to end at his death but instead expected to pass that control to future generations of Neumanns, too, says Business Insider.

The outlet reports that in a speech Neumann gave to employees in January of this year, footage of which it says it has viewed, Neumann is seen saying that WeWork isn’t “just controlled — we’re generationally controlled.” He reportedly goes on to say that while the five children he shares with wife Rebekah Neumann “don’t have to run the company,” they “do have to stay the moral compass of the company.”

According to BI, Neumann even invoked his future grandchildren, telling those gathered: “It’s important that one day, maybe in 100 years, maybe in 300 years, a great-great-granddaughter of mine will walk into that room and say, ‘Hey, you don’t know me; I actually control the place. The way you’re acting is not how we built it,’” he said.

These may sound like more outlandish proclamations from Neumann, who has a flair for the dramatic. (Talking to Fast Company earlier this year, he compared WeWork to a rare jewel, asking, “Do you know how long it takes a diamond to be created?”)

But before WeWork began coming apart at the seams, Neumann had every reason to believe that he could pass power down to his heirs.

#5297. Ripple-Backed Evernorth Cuts XRP Holdings by 60%

The Ripple-backed XRP treasury firm Evernorth has suffered substantial losses on its XRP ventures amid the persistent volatility facing the broad crypto market since the third quarter of 2026.

The firm has reported a massive write-down of its XRP holdings for Q3 2026 in a recent filing with the U.S. SEC, drawing attention from the broader crypto community.

On Tuesday, November 17, Evernorth reported a substantial decline in the value of its XRP holdings after the firm wrote down over $505 million in its latest financial filing with the SEC.

Notably, Evernorth issued a Form 10-Q for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, disclosing that it holds around 346 million XRP, now valued at about $342 million.

This has drawn attention across the XRP community and sparked discussions about the growing impact of persistent volatility on investors’ funds, as Evernorth’s XRP report marks a sharp drop from its initial valuation of $847 million.

Apparently, the firm reported that the tokens are now valued at about 40 cents per dollar of their initial worth. This means that the leading XRP treasury firm has reduced the value of its XRP holdings by nearly 60%.

It is important to note that the massive drop in the value of Evernorth’s XRP holdings does not mean that the firm has sold off its XRP. Rather, it marks a write-down in its previously listed XRP value.

The move may have been influenced by the persistent market drawdown, especially after XRP lost support at the key $1 level, closing steadily around $0.90 over the past few days.

Furthermore, Evernorth has specified that it has no intention of reversing the write-downs, even if the price of XRP later recovers.

#5296. Etzioni on AI: The outage conspiracy theories are wrong — our rush to patch and upgrade is the culprit

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 22, 2026 at 7:04 amNovember 22, 2026 at 7:06 am

In less than a week, Microsoft email went dark around the world, the FAA halted every departure in the country, Chase payments stalled, Apple’s services faltered and the NSA’s internal network went down. Sen. Josh Hawley said that if this was all a coincidence, “it’s like the greatest coincidence in the history of the world.” Yet intelligence and law enforcement officials told Congress they’ve found no evidence that anyone was attacking us.

Attackers typically announce when they’ve hit you. Terrorists claim credit. Criminals issue ransom notes and often brag as well: the hackers who crippled MGM’s casino systems in 2023 told TechCrunch within days. None of this month’s outages came with any of that.

Could a state actor be flexing its cyber capabilities to warn us? China’s Volt Typhoon hackers kept access to U.S. critical infrastructure for at least five years before anyone made it public, positioning themselves to disrupt it in a future crisis. However, hackers who are that patient don’t blow their cover by knocking out the world’s email. A warning shot also works only if the target knows who fired it, and we don’t have a credible suspect for a shooter here.

Each outage has a separate origin tracing back to the organization’s own systems: a new router a contractor was installing for the FAA, a bug Microsoft shipped in July, a software bug at Chase, an internal update at Apple, a patch at the NSA. To stage that, a single attacker would have to break into three companies and two federal agencies, disguise every intrusion as a routine mistake and leave nothing for investigators to find.

A far more credible root cause is the patch treadmill set at too high a speed: AI is finding security holes faster than anyone can safely fix them, and the rush to patch and upgrade is making everything more fragile. Think of an immune system in overdrive. It fights off infection, and sometimes it attacks healthy tissue. This month’s outages were a flare-up.

On Nov. 17, the startup Calif disclosed Java4Shell, a critical flaw in Java, the software platform used by government agencies and about 90% of Fortune 500 companies. Calif found it with OpenAI’s GPT-6 Cyber model. Oracle shipped a patch the same day, and a federal alert urged organizations to “immediately patch.”

Last month the same startup used OpenAI models to find a flaw in PHP, the programming language behind an estimated 70% of websites, and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton tied the NSA’s outage to the patching that followed. Microsoft alone fixed 1,413 vulnerabilities in October, more than its previous record for an entire year.

AI is forcing faster fixes. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella says his company’s outage came from a dormant bug, but he warned this week that AI-driven patching could bring more instability. AI has “allowed us to find these bugs and fix these bugs, but that means you’ve got to then patch them, and that creates instability,” he told CNBC.

A patch for a critical bank system might once have been tested for a week, he said at the New York Times DealBook Summit. Now it “needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild.”

The FBI warned on Nov. 13 that criminals and state-backed hackers are already using ARTEX, an open-source AI tool built for testing a company’s own defenses, with some intrusions going from first targeting to administrator-level access in under three hours. So the patching can’t slow down. Nobody would give up their immune system to avoid a flare-up.

It will get worse before it gets better. Calif’s CEO, Thai Duong, expects Java4Shell to threaten systems that don’t update for the next five to 10 years.

Meanwhile, the AI that finds flaws like this one is spreading. Open-weight models, which anyone can download and run without safeguards, trail the most advanced models on cyber tasks by only four to seven months, according to the UK AI Security Institute. Every month will bring more bugs, more emergency patches and more flare-ups.

There’s a finite amount of code in Windows, iOS and Chrome, and every bug AI finds and fixes there is one an attacker can’t use. Partners in Anthropic’s Project Glasswing, a program to secure critical software before AI can be turned against it, found more than 10,000 high- or critical-severity bugs in its first month.

Former Microsoft security staffer Angela Gunn sees a hopeful sign: more and more unrelated researchers are turning up the same bugs, which suggests the supply is finite. Fixing still lags finding, but the giants have the money and people to catch up. Within a year or two, I expect Windows, iOS and Chrome to be more secure than they’ve ever been.

A Bitcoin address that had not moved coins since February 2011 transferred 75 BTC on Nov. 17, according to Galaxy Research. At the current price of $64,935 per BTC, the coins are worth around $4.87 million.

The address is listed as a defendant in a $250 billion lawsuit in New York Supreme Court, in which the plaintiffs are trying to have early Bitcoin wallets declared "lost." Galaxy Research said that several other addresses from the same list have also moved coins in 2026.

According to Galaxy Research analysts, early on Nov. 17, in block 976,209, the address 1ALpEWtXApR19hLXvcG8NfkPyGsUMhFPMS sent coins for the first time. It was first funded on Feb. 8, 2011. At that time, Bitcoin was trading at about $0.90. After 15.8 years, the coins went to an unknown address with a 399-satoshi fee, or about 26 cents, for a paper gain of more than 7,000,000%.

Onchain databases list the wallet as Noah Doe #3409 (Salomon Client Dusted). That label is how it ended up among the defendants in the high-profile case ABC Company, XYZ Company, and Noah Doe v. John Does 1–39,069.

According to the lawsuit, an anonymous plaintiff using the pseudonym Noah Doe and two companies want the rights to 39,069 Bitcoin wallets that have not moved coins for more than five years. The plaintiffs said that these wallets hold about 3.8 million BTC, and at the current price, the coins are worth around $250 billion.

The plaintiffs filed the lawsuit under New York's lost-and-found law, Article 7-B of the Personal Property Law. Under the law, a person who finds lost property has to give it to the police, and the property goes to the finder if the owner does not claim it in time. In the lawsuit, the plaintiffs valued each address at less than $10, and they argued that the waiting period for such items was one year.

They "found" dormant addresses with an algorithm, saved them onto USB flash drives and took them to the New York Police Department (NYPD). Then they served the owners on the blockchain, through microtransactions with embedded messages (OP_RETURN). The practice is known as "dusting," and the campaign is tied to Salomon Brothers Strategic Advisors. Once the waiting period ran out, the plaintiffs asked the court to recognize the coins as theirs.

The case has been put on hold several times over motions to dismiss and amicus curiae briefs from outside experts. At a hearing on Sept. 8, the Bitcoin Policy Institute asked to intervene as a defendant, and The Digital Chamber asked to join the case as amicus curiae. Galaxy Research described it as a case "in which anonymous plaintiffs are seeking to claim legal title over Satoshi's coins."

Galaxy Research's Will Owens, who attended the hearing, said that The Digital Chamber's arguments were "well pleaded" and that "the judge sounded sympathetic to them."

Critics of the lawsuit argue that Article 7-B was written for things you can pick up and hand over for safekeeping. It wasn't written for blockchain records when the "finder" doesn't hold the private keys.

In September, Galaxy head of research Alex Thorn also said that the Lost and Found Property Law includes "protection from 'Noah Doe-style' dormancy attacks on legal ownership."

#5292. October 22, 2019

SoftBank founder Masayoshi Son vowed tonight to “double down” on its investment in WeWork as he confirmed plans for a $9.5 billion rescue package that will provide up to $1.7 billion to WeWork cofounder Adam Neumann in exchange for cutting most ties with the company and will give SoftBank an 80 percent stake in the business. In a statement tonight in New York, SoftBank said it would “accelerate” WeWork’s path to profitability and positive free cash flow. More here in the Financial Times.

Limited partners or LPs  — the pension funds, the university endowments, the family offices that largely provide venture firms with their spending money — are receiving a lot of attention from venture capitalists, some of it unwanted. VCs have begun knocking down their doors with requests for fresh capital commitments so they’ll have money to invest if the market cools down.

The problem is, many of these LPs are already over-allocated. LPs traditionally invest in many asset classes, such as public equities, and they allocate a small percentage of their portfolio to venture capital. Suddenly, they’re finding they’ve forked over more than they’d intended to VCs.

There are several reasons for this situation. First, VCs are returning to them ever faster for more capital  — sometimes in less than two years’ time  — because they are in vesting at such a furious pace.

Compounding the problem, not all LPs have received returns from their VC investments that they can recycle into new venture capital allocations. In some cases, this capital is still tied up in startups that are raising much more money than in the past and staying private longer. “We have some large exposures to blue chip names where IPOs have been rumored to be coming for a long time already, and now it’s maybe 2021, maybe 2022,” says one manager who asked not to be named. In other cases where startups have gone public, falling prices have prompted VCs to hang on to their shares instead of distribute them.

The result is that LPs are having to cut back on the number of managers they can fund, and that could mean bad news for venture capitalists and startups alike. These LPs don’t have much choice. As the LP explains it, “We have a pretty structured allocation process, and we’re really trying to be creative,” she says. One venture manager who reappeared too quickly for more money was  “easy to walk away from,” says this person. “Others, we’re having to do financial backflips for them to remain strong partners.” Either way, this LP adds, “We can’t add any new relationships right now,” meaning new venture teams in particular are out of luck. “When [VCs] shorten their fundraising cycle by nine months to a year, you can only squeeze the balloon so much.”

SoftBank’s $100 billion “Vision Fund” is one big reason LPs find themselves in their current predicament. From the moment SoftBank began waving money around several years ago, it launched a vicious cycle. According to Chris Douvos, whose investment firm, Ahoy Capital, owns stakes in such venture funds as True Ventures and First Round Capital, “When Andreessen Horowitz hit the scene a decade ago, they changed the tempo of investing and everyone got more aggressive in their dealmaking as a response. Then SoftBank entered the picture in a big way, and it was like a16z on steroids.”

#5291. Ripple-Backed Evernorth Takes Massive $505 Million XRP Hit

Ripple-backed XRP treasury company Evernorth Holdings has disclosed a significant decrease in the book value of its crypto asset holdings, with total impairment charges amounting to around $505 million before going public on Nasdaq.

Per an SEC filing on Nov. 13, the 346.3 million XRP tokens that Evernorth Holdings owned had a book value of just $341.9 million as of Sept. 30, 2026.

This is compared to the firm's initial accounting of the crypto assets at roughly $846.6 million, with an average acquisition or contribution price of $2.44 per XRP. This represents a nearly 60% decline in book value.

As per the latest filing, Evernorth recorded around $271 million in XRP impairment charges in the first nine months of 2026. This is in addition to the $233.7 million in impairment charges recorded in 2025.

Interestingly, only $6.9 million of the recent impairment charges occurred in the third quarter.

This also explains why Evernorth's XRP assets had a book value so far below their market value at the end of September.

Evernorth calculates impairments based on the lowest observable intraday price of XRP for each batch of tokens acquired. Once the assets are written down, the company is unable to reverse the previous losses if the price rises.

For reference, on Sept. 30, XRP closed the day trading at around $1.49 on Coinbase. At that price, Evernorth's 346.3 million XRP tokens would have been worth roughly $516 million, much higher than the disclosed book value of $341.9 million.

The recent disclosure comes around a month after Evernorth completed its business combination with Armada Acquisition Corp. II on Oct. 9. It started trading on Nasdaq under the symbol XRPN on Oct. 12.

Following the business combination, Evernorth held around 473 million XRP tokens and had also raised gross cash proceeds of around $300 million.

Its investors include Ripple, SBI Group, Arrington Capital, Pantera Capital, Kraken and GSR.

On Oct. 14, Evernorth announced collaborations with Ripple, Kraken, Coinbase and BitGo to implement institutional investment strategies starting in Q4 2026.

Meanwhile, its latest SEC filing did not include details on the amount of XRP deployed to generate yield or the returns generated from it.

A couple of years ago, the cofounder and CEO of a blood-testing company was publicly taken to task for implying in articles and professional profiles that he has a PhD when in reality, he’d left a prestigious graduate group three years after enrolling, without a degree.

The CEO is hardly alone in intentionally or otherwise sowing confusion around his credentials, however. Over the years, we’ve mistakenly believed that a number of founders have obtained specific college degrees based on their LinkedIn bio, only to learn offline that they enrolled for some period of time in a particular program that they didn’t complete.

It happened most recently with the cofounder of a startup who one would might surmise based on his LinkedIn profile has a master’s degree from Harvard but does not. We also misunderstood the CEO of a robotics company to have a PhD based on her LinkedIn. It was our fault; it mentioned under the credit that she’d left to start a company. But anyone scanning the site might have come to the same wrong conclusion. (We pointed this out to her team, and mention of the PhD was deleted.)

In a higher-profile case, James Damore, the fired Google engineer who authored that infamous memo about the company’s diversity practices and whose LinkedIn page cited under “Education” a “PhD, Systems Biology,” removed mention of those doctoral studies after Wired confirmed with Harvard that he was enrolled in the program but didn’t complete the doctorate.

Damore tried to defend his own LinkedIn profile, tweeting at the time, “I never told anyone I have a PhD. LinkedIn can’t distinguish between being in the PhD program and having a PhD (I forgot to update it).”

The round was led by Eldridge Industries, with participation from Evolution VC, and earlier backers Cota Capital, Lucas Venture Group, and YouTube cofounder Jawed Karim. More here.

The landmark catalyst unlocking this extreme upside is a highly unlikely but not impossible supercharged outcome of Tesla’s real progress on the Cybercab and Robotaxi platform.

Building on the recent opening of personal Cybercab orders at $29,990 (plus the required Autonomy Subscription) and the expansion of unsupervised Robotaxi service into additional cities with 24/7 operations, Tesla achieves rapid regulatory clearance and scales fully driverless operations across a much larger national (and early international) footprint far faster than expected.

TSLA has been trading in a wide range over recent months, with the stock recently pulling back from levels above $400 toward the high $380s–$390 area. Key support sits near $370–$380, with a stronger demand zone closer to $340–$350 if selling pressure intensifies.

Overhead resistance is layered around $410–$420 and then the more significant $450–$480 region that previously acted as a ceiling. Momentum has cooled after the recent decline, leaving the stock with room to reverse higher if buying interest returns.

While present price action reflects broader market caution and the typical volatility associated with Tesla, the company’s ongoing push into unsupervised autonomy continues to differentiate it.

The combination of real product progress on the Cybercab and Robotaxi and the theoretical potential for much faster-than-expected scaling creates a setup from which a parabolic re-rating remains possible.

Bank of America has disclosed a position in an XRP exchange-traded fund in its latest quarterly 13F filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. The filing, dated Nov. 16, shows that the bank held 13,260 shares of the futures-based Volatility Shares XRP ETF (XRPI), worth about $106,600, at the end of the third quarter.

Bank of America held 13,000 shares of the fund in the first quarter and 13,260 shares in the second quarter, according to its earlier 13F filings. The same filing lists more than $685 million in BlackRock's IBIT, $13.58 million in Bitwise and $950,000 in VanEck.

Seven major banks disclosed XRP fund holdings worth a total of $29.4 million in filings published between Nov. 9 and Nov. 16. Italy's Intesa Sanpaolo disclosed the largest stake among them, at $27.21 million. The bank held 712,319 shares of the Grayscale XRP Trust ETF, worth about $20.52 million, and it also opened a new position of 402,750 shares in the Bitwise XRP ETF, worth about $6.7 million.

UBS and Morgan Stanley disclosed XRP fund holdings of $1.91 million and $116,000, respectively. Most of the UBS position was in the Volatility Shares XRP ETF, and Morgan Stanley held funds from Franklin, REX-Osprey and Bitwise.

JPMorgan Chase held 539 shares of the Bitwise fund, worth about $9,000, and National Bank of Canada held 330 shares of the same fund, worth about $5,500. Bank of Montreal held REX-Osprey and ProShares Ultra XRP shares worth $4,300.

The crypto portfolio of Goldman Sachs grew to $2.64 billion by the end of September, according to its 13F filing. The bank held about $1.28 billion in Bitcoin ETFs, and BlackRock's IBIT and Fidelity's FBTC accounted for $778 million and $398 million of that amount, respectively. Goldman also held about $1.22 billion in Ether funds, and BlackRock's ETHA accounted for $603 million of that amount.

Goldman held $144 million in XRP ETFs at the end of the third quarter, up from $87 million at the end of the second quarter. The bank's 13F filing for the first quarter showed no XRP or Solana ETF holdings, and Goldman still held no Solana funds at the end of September.

The bank held shares of five spot XRP funds from Franklin Templeton, Bitwise, Canary, Grayscale and 21Shares, and its Franklin Templeton position was worth almost $48 million.

Besides, trading firm Jane Street reported $23.5 million in XRP funds, and Simplex Trading disclosed a $14 million stake in the Grayscale fund. EP Wealth Advisors raised its Volatility Shares XRP ETF holding by 37% to 18,400 shares, worth about $148,000.

A 13F filing only shows long positions as of Sept. 30. It doesn't show whether the banks hedge those holdings with shorts, or what they did with the shares in October and November. Since then, XRP has fallen below $1, and on Tuesday morning, XRP was trading at $0.966.

#5286. Bitcoin's $90,000 Comeback Now Unlikely, Novogratz Warns

Galaxy Digital CEO Mike Novogratz said that the odds of Bitcoin hitting $90,000 by the end of 2026 are slim in light of prevailing macroeconomic headwinds and the growing likelihood that the Federal Reserve may hike interest rates.

During a live event with Anthony Scaramucci at the Digital Assets Forum in New York City, Novogratz was asked if Bitcoin could get back to $90,000 by the end of this year.

"Less likely than it was. You need something to happen," Novogratz said.

His gloomy outlook comes as Bitcoin has struggled to rebound after a devastating drop that saw its price dip as low as $62,000 over the weekend. Bitcoin's price stood at around $64,600 on Nov. 17. The largest cryptocurrency by market capitalization has declined for six consecutive weeks.

A shift in the U.S. monetary policy outlook, namely the prospect of more rate hikes from the Federal Reserve, has been largely to blame for Bitcoin's decline, according to Novogratz.

"At the start of the year, everybody thought the Fed was going to be cutting now," he said.

But high inflation and ongoing supply shocks have forced investors to readjust their expectations.

"Inflation's going up. We've got inflation going up," Novogratz said, warning that inflationary pressures could become increasingly entrenched.

"The Fed's going to hike. At least two more, probably three more," he said.

Novogratz predicted that the Fed would raise rates by 25 basis points in December and then hike again at its next meeting.

He said that higher rates, at least in the near term, tend to weigh on Bitcoin. But the higher cost of government borrowing could eventually provide support for the cryptocurrency.

"Yeah, later," he said in response to the suggestion that higher borrowing costs could be a tailwind for Bitcoin.

"First, you're gonna hike rates. Oh, sell gold, right? You're going to go to the dollar. It's so ingrained in peoples' heads," he said.

"Carry costs going up," he said. Bitcoin doesn't offer the same yield as interest-bearing dollar assets.

"You don't make any interest on Bitcoin in dollars," he said.

In particular, Novogratz said that the massive rise in Treasury yields has been particularly detrimental to the crypto market.

"Literally 40 basis points in like four days of trading. So that's why crypto's down," he said.

He also said that the massive crypto hack could still be weighing on investors' minds, adding to market jitters.

"I think in the back of their minds is the hack," he said.
